summary: Describes a Telnet option that lets a client tell a Telnet server how large its window is. It was a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1073 proposes a Telnet option that lets the client report its window width and height to the server. The client can send the dimensions again after a resize, but the information is advisory.

how does telnet send terminal size
how does telnet send window size
subtitle: How a Telnet client tells a server the size of its terminal window.

tldr.problem: A server may need a terminal window's current width and height to control a display, especially when the user resizes it.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server negotiate NAWS, after which the client sends width and height as two 16-bit values and may send updates.
tldr.outcome: The option provides advisory window-size information from the client to the server; the server may choose not to use it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1073's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC describes NAWS as a proposed Telnet option.

sections.title: Why the Server Needs Window Size
sections.content:
A Telnet client may run inside a window whose dimensions can change. The server may need to know those dimensions to control the terminal display and adjust output after a resize.

The RFC proposes NAWS, or Negotiate About Window Size, to send the current width and height from client to server. The information is advisory, so the server may accept the option without using the values.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can tell the server how much screen space it has. This helps the server adjust output when the window changes size.

sections.title: Agreeing to Exchange Dimensions
sections.content:
The client can suggest NAWS with IAC WILL NAWS, and the server can request it with IAC DO NAWS. The other side accepts or refuses using the standard Telnet negotiation commands.

After agreement, the client sends a subnegotiation containing the size. The server may later send DON'T NAWS if it cannot handle further updates, which the RFC says avoids a negotiation loop.
sections.plainLanguage: The two Telnet programs first agree to use the option. Only then does the client send the window dimensions.

sections.title: Sending Width and Height
sections.content:
The subnegotiation carries width and height as two 16-bit values, each sent in two bytes. A value of zero means that the corresponding dimension is not being sent, and the server chooses an operating-system-specific value.

The largest value for either dimension is 65535 characters. As required by Telnet, a data byte with value 255 is doubled so it is not mistaken for the IAC command byte.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends two numbers: the window width and height in characters. A zero says that one dimension is unknown or omitted.
